title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students used ChatGPT to support knowledge building in a World Religions course and how that experience related to their developing AI literacy. The authors are motivated by a gap in K-12 AI education research: there are many proposals for teaching AI literacy and many tools for using AI in learning, but few empirical studies describe students’ actual processes and understandings when working with generative AI.

The study was conducted in a knowledge-building classroom where the teacher intentionally integrated ChatGPT into two phases of instruction. In the first phase, ChatGPT was used to generate a sample essay and a pool of inquiry questions that students critiqued, compared, and used to launch their own investigations. In the second phase, students used a teacher-designed steering prompt to ask ChatGPT questions, then fact-checked responses, discussed them with peers, posted reflections on Knowledge Forum, and used the resulting ideas in essays and collaborative notes. The intervention was supported by teacher planning, classroom discussion, and explicit guidance on prompt engineering, citation, and ethical use.

Participants were one teacher and 10 high school students from an elective World Religions course in a major South American city; students came from three schools and were mostly from upper-middle-class families. Data came from student interviews, student artifacts from Miro and Knowledge Forum, and teacher planning/reflection documents. The study finds that students used ChatGPT for information search, idea generation, support for writing, and quick clarification, but they also encountered challenges such as hallucinations, difficulty fact-checking, and limitations in prompt quality. Over time, students developed a more nuanced understanding of ChatGPT’s strengths, weaknesses, risks, and social implications, although their understanding of AI mechanisms remained mostly rudimentary. The authors conclude that carefully scaffolded integration of GenAI in knowledge building can support both disciplinary learning and emerging AI literacy, but students need structured opportunities to critique, verify, and reflect on AI output.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom study using semi-structured interviews, student artifacts, and teacher notes, with strong descriptive coding but no experimental comparison or causal identification. It is peer-reviewed/in press and methodologically coherent, but it provides evidence of processes and perceptions rather than measurable learning effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for information efficiency, collaboration, and AI literacy in a small K-12 sample, but it reports no effect sizes or direct learning gains. The impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude for broader populations.

interventions.use_case: Classroom integration of ChatGPT as a conversational AI used by high school students to ask questions, generate ideas, brainstorm inquiry questions, draft essays, and receive brief follow-up prompts during a World Religions knowledge-building unit.

finding.finding_summary: The study qualitatively found that ChatGPT supported students’ domain learning in world religions by helping them search for information, surface multiple perspectives, and generate inquiry questions and essay ideas. Students reported using ChatGPT to support understanding and knowledge construction rather than as a direct source of final answers; however, the paper does not report standardized achievement scores, so no effect size is available (n=10 interviewed students).
finding.measure: Student interviews; student artifacts on Miro and Knowledge Forum; teacher planning/reflective notes

finding.finding_summary: The strongest documented outcome was improved critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, and collaboration in a Knowledge Building context. Students described fact-checking ChatGPT outputs, comparing AI-generated and peer-generated ideas, and reflecting on the strengths, weaknesses, and trustworthiness of AI; these are qualitative findings from interviews with n=10 students, not quantified with effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student interviews; coded reflections on AI use; Knowledge Forum posts and transcripts

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported that ChatGPT improved task efficiency by making information search faster, generating concise summaries, helping with outlines, and supporting quick responses during class. About 70% of participants said it improved information searching, but the paper provides no experimental comparison or quantitative achievement metric.
finding.measure: Student interview reports of time-saving and task completion support

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed both enthusiasm and concern about ChatGPT, indicating mixed social-emotional responses: some found it personal and motivating, while others worried about overreliance, distraction, and misuse. The study is qualitative and does not provide a quantitative measure of engagement or motivation; the evidence comes from interview themes across n=10 students.
finding.measure: Student interview themes about trust, concern, motivation, and perceived danger
